items.followUp: Write the equation for the reaction of methane with chlorine in diffused sunlight.

rubric.why: The reactants and their coefficients must be correct for the bright-sunlight reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing methane and two molecules of chlorine as the reactants.

rubric.why: These are the products of the balanced reaction in bright sunlight.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing carbon and four molecules of hydrogen chloride.

modelAnswer: In bright sunlight, methane reacts explosively with chlorine:
CH₄ + 2Cl₂ → C + 4HCl.
This is a balanced equation.
The reaction is a substitution reaction.
Bright sunlight causes the reaction to proceed explosively, forming carbon and hydrogen chloride.
A similar reaction in diffused sunlight is: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
The bright-sunlight equation is the one asked for.
The products are carbon and hydrogen chloride.
The balanced equation is CH₄ + 2Cl₂ → C + 4HCl.
Answer: CH₄ + 2Cl₂ → C + 4HCl.

items.followUp: Define a molecular formula and give the molecular and empirical formulas of hydrogen peroxide.

rubric.why: A molecular formula gives the actual number of each type of atom in a molecule.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for explaining that it shows the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.

rubric.why: An empirical formula represents the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for defining it as the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element.

rubric.why: The examples illustrate how molecular and empirical formulas differ.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct molecular and corresponding empirical formula pair.

modelAnswer: A molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.
For example, the molecular formula of glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆.
An empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
The empirical formula of glucose is CH₂O.
For hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂ is the molecular formula and HO is the empirical formula.

items.followUp: Describe the discharge-tube experiment that showed cathode rays travel from the cathode towards the anode.

rubric.why: The rays were investigated using a discharge tube.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the discharge tube (Crookes tube).

rubric.why: The experiment used gas at low pressure and an electrical discharge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning low-pressure gas and a high-voltage electrical discharge.

rubric.why: A glow on the tube wall provided evidence of the rays and their path.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a glow or fluorescence caused by rays originating at the cathode and moving towards the anode.

rubric.why: Cathode rays were identified as negatively charged particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying cathode rays as negatively charged particles (electrons).

modelAnswer: Cathode rays were observed in a discharge tube containing gas at very low pressure.
A high voltage was applied between the electrodes in the tube.
A glow appeared on the glass wall, showing that rays travelled from the cathode towards the anode.
The rays were called cathode rays and were found to consist of negatively charged particles (electrons).

items.followUp: Explain the formation of an ionic bond between magnesium and oxygen, showing the ions formed.

rubric.why: An ionic bond is formed through electron transfer and electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining an ionic bond as attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.

rubric.why: A sodium atom loses its outer electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sodium loses one electron.

rubric.why: A chlorine atom gains the electron lost by sodium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorine gains one electron.

rubric.why: Electron transfer produces a positive sodium ion and a negative chloride ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly showing Na⁺ and Cl⁻; correct electron arrangements may also be credited.

rubric.why: The attraction between the ions holds them together in sodium chloride.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the attraction between the oppositely charged ions to formation of NaCl.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by transfer of electron(s).
A sodium atom has the electronic arrangement 2,8,1 and loses one electron: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻.
A chlorine atom has the electronic arrangement 2,8,7 and gains that electron: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻.
Sodium and chloride ions are formed: Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
Their opposite charges attract, forming an ionic bond in sodium chloride, NaCl.

items.followUp: Define solubility and state how increasing temperature affects the solubility of solids and gases in water.

rubric.why: Solubility is a maximum amount defined for a specified quantity of solvent and temperature in a saturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for stating that it is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent to form a saturated solution at a specified temperature.

rubric.why: The solubility of most solid solutes increases as temperature rises.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing temperature generally increases the solubility of solids.

rubric.why: Gas solubility in liquids generally decreases as temperature rises.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing temperature generally decreases the solubility of gases.

modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent to form a saturated solution at a specified temperature.
The solubility of most solid substances in water increases as the temperature increases.
The solubility of gases in water generally decreases as the temperature increases.

items.followUp: Define organic chemistry and give one example of an organic compound.

rubric.why: Organic chemistry deals with hydrocarbons and their derivatives (organic carbon compounds).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining organic chemistry as the study of hydrocarbons and their derivatives or organic carbon compounds.

rubric.why: Methane is a valid example of an organic compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a correct example, such as methane (CH₄).

modelAnswer: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
Methane (CH₄) is an example of an organic compound.

items.followUp: Differentiate between the atomic number and mass number of an atom.

rubric.why: The atomic number is determined by the number of protons in the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atomic number equals the number of protons in the nucleus.

rubric.why: The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons.

modelAnswer: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Atomic mass (mass number) is the total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus.

rubric.why: Conservation of mass number and atomic number gives carbon-12 as one product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the carbon-12 nucleus, ¹²₆C.

rubric.why: The remaining product is a proton, ¹₁H.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the proton product.
